title: Fossil Poop and Footprints: The Clues Dinosaurs Left Behind
summary:
When you think of fossils, you probably picture a dinosaur skeleton in a museum. But there's another kind of fossil that's just as cool: trace fossils. These aren't body parts—they're records of what ancient animals did. We're talking footprints, burrows, nests, and even poop and vomit.

Trace fossils form when an animal leaves a mark in mud or sand, and that mark gets buried and turned to stone over millions of years. Scientists called ichnologists study these clues to learn about daily life in the past.

For example, fossilized poop, called coprolites, can show what a creature ate. One coprolite revealed that pterosaurs—flying reptiles—ate mollusks and crustaceans over 150 million years ago. Another showed that Ice Age squirrels may have snacked on woolly mammoth remains.

Footprints can even tell us how fast dinosaurs ran. And burrows found in Taiwan suggest giant worms hid under the seafloor and ambushed prey, like the monster in Star Wars.

So next time you see a footprint in mud, think about what it might become in 100 million years!
why_it_matters: It shows that even small things — like a footprint in mud today — can become important science far in the future.

background_read: Taiwan (a small island in East Asia) is where scientists found those ancient burrows under the seafloor.
During the Ice Age (a long, cold time when huge sheets of ice covered much of the Earth), woolly mammoths — elephant-like animals with long hair — roamed the land.
Fossils form when mud, sand, or ash buries something and, over millions of years, slowly hardens into rock.
Article_Structure: WHO: Ichnologists — scientists who study trace fossils — are the ones reading these clues.
WHAT: Footprints, burrows, nests, poop, and vomit from long ago are fossils too, and they show how animals lived.
WHERE: In mud and sand that turned to stone, including burrows found in Taiwan.
WHY: These marks reveal what ancient animals ate, how fast they ran, and how they hunted, even when no bones were found.

perspectives.description: They are thrilled that poop and footprints can tell stories that bones alone cannot.
They might think a skeleton is more exciting than a footprint until they hear what the footprint proves.
They warn that we must be sure the mark was really made by an animal and not by weather or moving mud.
